To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

prescribed burning of big sagebrush communities in south-central Montana resulted in increased use of burned areas by elk for 15  years following burning, and that the increased use was associated with increased forage biomass and protein levels.

prescribed burning of big sagebrush communities in south-central Montana increased elk use of the burned area for at least 15 years and resulted in higher production and protein content of forages for at least 10 years, but did not result in increased plant diversity.
burning sagebrush communities leads to increases in elk use and forage production that persist for at least 15 years.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of burning on plant community structure, forage production and nutritional quality, and use by elk in big sagebrush-dominated shrub communities of south-central Montana.
how changes in plant communities and forage quality following burning affect herbivore use.
the short- and long-term responses of elk and plant communities in sagebrush steppe to prescribed burning.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
elk use increased on burned sites, but it was difficult to determine the relative contribution of changes in plant biomass, plant protein, plant community structure, or plant community composition.
prescribed burning of mountain big sagebrush communities in the northern Great Basin resulted in increased elk use of burned areas up to 15 years post-burn.

prescribed burning of sagebrush-dominated communities can lead to long-term increases in plant production, protein levels, and elk use, but that these responses may be more complex than previously recognized.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
burning increased forage production and nutritional quality for elk, and elk responded by using burned areas more heavily than control areas for up to 15 years after burning.
elk used areas more intensively following burning and that this was related to changes in plant communities and plant production.
burning of big sagebrush communities leads to increases in herbaceous plant species, forage production and protein, and elk forage use.
The main takeaway from our work is that
burning can lead to long-term increases in elk use and forage quality and that the effects of burning can persist for at least 15 years in sagebrush communities.
burning sagebrush communities can lead to long-term changes in elk use and plant production.
prescribed burning can be used to transform sagebrush communities into native herb communities that persist for many years without sagebrush reinvasions.
